<!-- Generated by `khora doc` from the `///` and `//!` comments in `std::net::http`. Edits here are overwritten; change the source. -->

HTTP/1.1, over the sockets in `std::net::socket`. Both directions.

The specification does not define `std::net::http`; the shape here was
reconstructed from how the reference application uses it, and every line
below it is Khora over `String::slice`, `String::index_of` and `Map`.

**Answering**: a request line with its query string, headers, a body read
to the length the headers promised, routing on method and path with `:name`
segments, and a response that can carry headers of its own. On a fiber per
connection, which took a language feature to reach rather than a line here
— see `Router::serve_once`.

**Asking**: `HttpClient`, a capability, from `Call` to `Answer`. A service
that cannot call another service is not one, and this half arrived a long
way after the first.

What neither does: content negotiation, multipart bodies, compression, or
following a redirect. Each is absent deliberately rather than forgotten.
Chunked transfer is *read* by the client and not written by the server,
which is the split real traffic has: a response of unknown length is
ordinary and a request of unknown length is not.

A connection is reached through a `Transport`, which is three closures, so
that the serving path is written once, `Router::listen` and
`Router::listen_tls` differ only in what they hand it, and the client
reuses both without knowing which it has.

## Types

### Method

```khora
pub type Method =
  | Get
  | Post
  | Put
  | Patch
  | Delete;
```

The five verbs this server routes on.

Not every verb HTTP defines: `HEAD`, `OPTIONS` and `TRACE` are answered by
the server rather than routed to a handler, and a method nobody can mount a
route for is not worth a case here. `of` returns `None` for the rest, which
becomes a 400 rather than a panic.

### Params

```khora
pub type Params = {
  bound: Map<String, String>,
};
```

The path parameters a route matched: `/analyze/:account_id` against
`/analyze/acc_9921` binds `account_id`.

### Request

```khora
pub type Request = {
  method: Method,
  path: String,
  params: Params,
  queries: Map<String, String>,
  headers: Map<String, String>,
  body: String,
};
```

One request, parsed: the verb, the path, what the route bound, the query,
the headers and the body.

**Everything is decoded on arrival**, once. A handler reading three query
parameters and two headers does no parsing at all — the maps below are
already built, and the header names are already lowercased.

#### path

```khora
path: String
```

The path with the query string taken off: `/analyze/acc_1?deep=true` has
a path of `/analyze/acc_1`. Routes match against this, so mounting
`/analyze/:id` does not stop working the moment a client adds a
parameter.

#### queries

```khora
queries: Map<String, String>
```

Decoded once, when the request arrives, rather than on every lookup — a
handler that reads three parameters should not decode the query three
times.

#### headers

```khora
headers: Map<String, String>
```

Keyed by the **lowercased** name, because HTTP header names are
case-insensitive and a map is not. Folding the case here rather than in
`header` means two headers differing only in case collide on arrival,
which is the correct reading: they are the same header.

### Header

```khora
pub type Header = {
  name: String,
  value: String,
};
```

One header on the way out.

### Response

```khora
pub type Response = {
  status: Int,
  body: String,
  content_type: String,
  headers: List<Header>,
};
```

What a handler answers with: a status, a body, its type, and any extra
headers.

`json` and `text` build the two common ones. `with_header` adds to either,
and returns a new response rather than changing the one it was given.

#### headers

```khora
headers: List<Header>
```

Anything beyond the three a response always carries. A list rather than a
map, because `Set-Cookie` may legitimately appear more than once and a
map would silently keep only the last.

### HttpError

```khora
derive(Show, Eq)
pub type HttpError =
  | BindFailed(port: Int)
  | MalformedRequest(details: String);
```

What can go wrong that is the *server's* problem rather than a client's.

A malformed request from a client is answered with a 400 and never reaches
here — that is a response, not an error. These two are the cases where
there is nobody to answer: the port would not bind, or a request could not
be read at all.

### RequestLine

```khora
pub type RequestLine = {
  method: Method,
  target: String,
};
```

The first line of a request, before the target has been split.

Public because a caller parsing a request for its own reasons wants the
target as the client wrote it; `Request` carries the split version.

#### target

```khora
target: String
```

The request target as written, query string and all. `parse` splits it;
keeping it whole here means a caller reading a request line for its own
reasons gets what the client actually sent.

### Transport

```khora
pub type Transport = {
  receive: (Array<U8>) -> Int,
  transmit: (String) -> Int,
  shut: () -> (),
};
```

How to speak to one client, whatever is underneath.

**Three closures rather than a socket handle**, because a plain connection
and a TLS one differ in exactly these three operations and in nothing else
the router does. Before this the serving path took an `Int`, which is a
socket, and there was no way to put a handshake in front of it without
writing the whole path twice.

The cost is two indirect calls per request — one read, one write — against a
parse that performs several hundred reference-count operations. It did not
move the benchmark.

A record of closures is what an `effect` compiles to anyway
([the effect-runtime design note](https://github.com/codyspate/khoralang/blob/main/docs/design/effect-runtime.md) §2), and this is not one only because a
transport belongs to a connection rather than to a computation: two fibers
serve two clients at once, and a capability installed by `with` would be
one of them.

#### receive

```khora
receive: (Array<U8>) -> Int
```

Bytes into the buffer: how many, 0 when the peer closed, or -1.

#### transmit

```khora
transmit: (String) -> Int
```

The text, all of it, or -1.

#### shut

```khora
shut: () ->()
```

Ends the conversation and releases whatever is underneath.

### Connection

```khora
pub type Connection = {
  transport: Transport,
  buffer: Array<U8>,
  mut carried: Int,
};
```

One connection, read a request at a time.

**This is the layer between a socket and a router**, and it is public
because a router is a matter of taste and this is not. Framing a request
correctly — reading until it is whole, honouring `Content-Length`, holding
what a pipelined client sent early, refusing one that will not fit — is the
same work whatever shape the framework above it has, and it is the work that
fails in production rather than in testing.

`Router` is written against this and has no privileged access to anything
below it. A framework with a different shape — middleware chain, effect
handler, one function per method — starts here and owes nothing to `Router`.

**Nothing here spawns.** A connection is read by whoever calls `next`, on
whatever fiber that is. `Router` gives each connection a fiber in its accept
loop and that is a decision of the accept loop, not of this type: a server
that answers one caller at a time, or hands connections to a pool, is
written against exactly this.

#### carried

```khora
mut carried: Int
```

Bytes of the *next* request that arrived with the last one. A pipelining
client sends two without waiting, and the second must not be dropped.

### Incoming

```khora
pub type Incoming =
  | Arrived(request: Request, keep: Bool)
  | Ended
  | Rejected(response: Response);
```

What reading a connection produced.

#### Arrived

```khora
| Arrived(request: Request, keep: Bool)
```

A whole request, and whether the client asked to keep the connection open.

The flag is read from the `Connection` header here rather than by the
caller, because the caller would have to fold the header's case and this
has already done it.

#### Ended

```khora
| Ended
```

The peer closed, or the read deadline passed. There is nothing to answer
and nothing to send.

#### Rejected

```khora
| Rejected(response: Response)
```

Nothing usable arrived: send this and close.

A client that could not be understood cannot be trusted about where its
next request begins, so the connection cannot be reused whatever the
`Connection` header said.

### Route

```khora
pub type Route<'er> = {
  method: Method,
  pattern: String,
  handler: SharedFn<Request, Response, 'er>,
};
```

One mounted route.

The handler is a `SharedFn` rather than a plain closure, and that is what
lets a router be answered on a fiber of its own. A closure's captures are
not in its type, so a record holding one can never be handed to another
fiber; `SharedFn::of` checks the captures where the closure is written and
hands back something that has forgotten it was ever a closure.

It also takes the capabilities out of the router's type. A handler closes
over what it needs at the mount site, so there is no `'r` left for a `Route`
to carry — `Router<'er>` says only how its handlers can fail.

### Router

```khora
pub type Router<'er> = {
  routes: List<Route<'er>>,
};
```

A router carries its handlers' failures, so mounting a route that can fail
against the database widens the router's own error row.

### Url

```khora
pub type Url = {
  secure: Bool,
  host: String,
  port: Int,
  target: String,
};
```

Where a call is going.

#### secure

```khora
secure: Bool
```

Whether to put TLS in front of the socket.

#### target

```khora
target: String
```

Path and query, together, beginning with `/`. What goes on the request
line unchanged — a client that re-encodes what it was given is a client
that breaks somebody's signed URL.

### Call

```khora
pub type Call = {
  method: Method,
  url: String,
  headers: List<Header>,
  body: String,
};
```

A request this program is making.

#### headers

```khora
headers: List<Header>
```

A list rather than a map, matching `Response`: two headers of the same
name are legal on the way out and a map would keep one.

### Answer

```khora
pub type Answer = {
  status: Int,
  headers: Map<String, String>,
  body: String,
};
```

What came back.

Headers keyed by the **lowercased** name, as `Request`'s are and for the
same reason: HTTP header names are case-insensitive and a map is not.

### CallError

```khora
derive(Show, Eq)
pub type CallError =
  | BadUrl(String)
  | Unreachable(String)
  | Insecure(String)
  | Closed(String)
  | Malformed(String)
  | TooLarge(Int)
  | Denied(String);
```

What can go wrong reaching somebody else.

Separate from `HttpError`, which is what goes wrong *being* a server —
a port that would not bind, a request that could not be read. Nothing that
matches one has any use for the cases of the other.

#### BadUrl

```khora
| BadUrl(String)
```

The URL could not be read.

#### Unreachable

```khora
| Unreachable(String)
```

No connection: the name did not resolve, or nothing answered.

#### Insecure

```khora
| Insecure(String)
```

The TLS handshake did not complete.

#### Closed

```khora
| Closed(String)
```

The peer went away before the answer was whole.

#### Malformed

```khora
| Malformed(String)
```

Something arrived and it was not an HTTP answer this can read.

#### TooLarge

```khora
| TooLarge(Int)
```

The answer was longer than the client was willing to hold.

#### Denied

```khora
| Denied(String)
```

The manifest does not grant this host.

**Its own case, not `Unreachable`.** The two send a reader to different
places: `Unreachable` is DNS, a firewall, a service that is down, and
`Denied` is `[permissions] network` in `khora.toml`. Reported as
`host:port` so the line that would allow it can be copied out of the
message.

## Effects

### HttpClient

```khora
pub effect HttpClient {
  send: (Call) -> Result<Answer, CallError>,
}
```

Making requests, as a capability.

**An effect rather than a function**, for the reason `std::db`'s `Db` is
one. A program that says `with { http: HttpClient }` can be handed a
recording double in a test, a client that only reaches one host, or one
wrapped for tracing — and every caller above is unchanged, because a
capability *is* an interception point. [The observability design note](https://github.com/codyspate/khoralang/blob/main/docs/design/observability.md) shows
the wrapper.

One operation. `Call` carries everything a request is, so a second would
only be a shorter way to build one, and `Call::get` is already that.

#### send

```khora
send: (Call) -> Result<Answer, CallError>
```

### Request

```khora
impl Request
```

#### get

```khora
pub fn get(path: String) -> Request
```

A GET request for `path`, with no parameters matched yet. Chiefly for
tests: a real one arrives from a socket.

#### post

```khora
pub fn post(path: String, body: String) -> Request
```

A POST to `path` carrying `body`. For tests, like `get`.

#### of

```khora
pub fn of(method: Method, target: String, body: String) -> Request
```

The query string is honoured here too, so a hand-built request behaves
like one off the wire. A test that writes `Request::get("/x?a=1")` and
finds no `a` would be testing the constructor rather than the code.

#### query

```khora
pub fn query(self, name: String) -> Option<String>
```

A query parameter, already percent-decoded.

A parameter written with no `=` — `/x?verbose` — is present with an empty
value, which is how every server reads it and what lets a handler ask
"was this requested" rather than "what does it say".

#### header

```khora
pub fn header(self, name: String) -> Option<String>
```

A header, by a name in any case.

`Host`, `host` and `HOST` are one header. The RFC says so, and this is
the half of it that everybody gets wrong.

### Response

```khora
impl Response
```

#### json

```khora
pub fn json<A: Encode>(status: Int, body: A) -> Response
```

Encodes `body` as JSON and sends it with the given status.

`A: Encode`, so a derived record, a `Json` built by hand and a list of
`Rejection`s all serve: `Response::json(422, problems)` is the body a
client reads a refused request from. A record holding a secret has no
`Encode`, so it cannot be sent by accident.

#### text

```khora
pub fn text(status: Int, body: String) -> Response
```

`body` as `text/plain`, with the given status.

#### with_header

```khora
pub fn with_header(self, name: String, value: String) -> Response
```

The same response with one more header on it.

A new response rather than a mutated one, like `Prompt`'s builders and
for the same reason: a half-built response cannot be shared and then
changed underneath its other holder.

#### rendered

```khora
pub fn rendered(self) -> String
```

The response, as bytes on the wire.

#### rendered_keeping

```khora
pub fn rendered_keeping(self, keep: Bool) -> String
```

The same, saying whether the connection is staying open.

**Reuse is worth two orders of magnitude and nothing else here is.**
Measured on this machine, one server answering the same request: 6,116 a
second on a fresh connection each time, 1,129,782 on one held open. The
handshake, the teardown and the port churn were the whole cost; the
server was never the bottleneck. That is also why comparing this to a
server benchmarked with keep-alive was comparing two different questions.

`Content-Length` is on every response already, which is what makes this
safe: a client knows where the body ends and where the next answer
begins without the connection closing to tell it.

#### reason

```khora
pub fn reason(status: Int) -> String
```

The reason phrase for a status.

The ones a service actually sends, which has twice turned out to be more
than the list had. The link shortener answered a redirect and got
`HTTP/1.1 302 Unknown` on the wire; later a service under load answered
503 and got the same. A phrase is advisory — every client reads the
number — but one that says `Unknown` about a status the server
deliberately chose reads as a bug to whoever is holding the packet
capture, and it was.

**The whole of 5xx is here now**, because that is the family a server
sends about *itself*: 503 under backpressure, 502 and 504 from anything
with a proxy in front of it, 501 for a method it does not implement.
Those are the lines somebody reads at three in the morning.

A `match` rather than a chain of `else if`s. Twenty-seven of them in a
row is a table pretending to be control flow, and a table should look
like one -- the numbers are in order here, so a missing status is
something a reader can see rather than something they have to search for.

413 stays "Payload Too Large" although RFC 9110 renames it "Content Too
Large". That is a wire string somebody may be matching on, and changing
it is a decision of its own rather than something to slip into a list of
additions.

### Connection

```khora
impl Connection
```

#### over

```khora
pub fn over(transport: Transport) -> Connection
```

Over a transport, holding at most [`default_limit`] bytes per request.

#### holding

```khora
pub fn holding(transport: Transport, most: Int) -> Connection
```

The same, with a cap of your own.

The buffer is allocated once for the connection rather than once per
request, so this is what one caller costs in memory for as long as they
are connected.

#### next

```khora
pub fn next(self) -> Incoming
```

Reads until one request is whole, and says what arrived.

Blocks. Whether that blocks a thread, a fiber or the only thread there is
belongs to the caller — see the note on [`Connection`].

#### understood

```khora
pub fn understood(text: String) -> Incoming
```

Parses one request, or the 400 to answer it with.

Everything a connection needs to decide before a handler runs: whether
the bytes were a request at all, and — from the headers the parser has
already folded — whether the client asked to keep the connection.

#### reply

```khora
pub fn reply(self, response: Response, keep: Bool) -> Int
```

Renders `response` and sends it.

`keep` decides the `Connection` header, and is what [`Incoming::Arrived`]
reported unless the caller has its own reason to close.

The two travel together because they are decided together: the answer's
status and the request's `Connection` header are both known once, at the
point the request has been parsed, and working either out again afterwards
means reading the request a second time.

#### shut

```khora
pub fn shut(self) ->()
```

Ends the conversation and releases the transport.

### Router

```khora
impl Router
```

Mounting is written `router |> Router::post(..)`, so the router is the
first parameter of each. They are the type's own functions rather than free
ones so that the pipeline reads as a chain against `Router` and cannot
collide with another module's `get`.

One per method, over a general `on` that takes the method as a value. Both
are worth having: the named five are what a pipeline reads best with, and
`on` is what stops the set being closed — a router with only the verbs
somebody thought to write helpers for is the shape this had before, and it
made a REST service unwritable.

#### new

```khora
pub fn new<'er>() -> Router<'er>
```

A router with no routes. The start of the pipeline.

#### on

```khora
pub fn on<'er>(router: Router<'er>, method: Method, route: String, handler: SharedFn<Request, Response, 'er>) -> Router<'er>
```

Mounts `handler` at `route` for `method`.

**The general one, and the five below are it with a name.** A router that
could only mount the methods somebody had written a helper for is a
router that stops at whatever its first caller needed — which is what
this one did, for months, with `get` and `post` and no way to say `PUT`
at all. The named five exist because `Router::get(..)` reads better in a
pipeline than `Router::on(Method::Get, ..)`, not because they are the
only ones allowed.

Later mounts are tried first, because each prepends. Mounting the same
route twice is allowed and the second one wins, which is worth knowing
rather than an invariant anything enforces.

#### get

```khora
pub fn get<'er>(router: Router<'er>, route: String, handler: SharedFn<Request, Response, 'er>) -> Router<'er>
```

Mounts `handler` at `route` for GET.

#### post

```khora
pub fn post<'er>(router: Router<'er>, route: String, handler: SharedFn<Request, Response, 'er>) -> Router<'er>
```

Mounts `handler` at `route` for POST.

#### put

```khora
pub fn put<'er>(router: Router<'er>, route: String, handler: SharedFn<Request, Response, 'er>) -> Router<'er>
```

Mounts `handler` at `route` for PUT.

#### patch

```khora
pub fn patch<'er>(router: Router<'er>, route: String, handler: SharedFn<Request, Response, 'er>) -> Router<'er>
```

Mounts `handler` at `route` for PATCH.

#### delete

```khora
pub fn delete<'er>(router: Router<'er>, route: String, handler: SharedFn<Request, Response, 'er>) -> Router<'er>
```

Mounts `handler` at `route` for DELETE.

`delete` rather than `remove`, because the method is spelled `DELETE` and
a router's job is to say what the wire says.

#### listen

```khora
pub fn listen<'er>(router: Router<'er>, port: Int) ->() raises 'er + HttpError + ChildFailed
```

Serves until the process stops, on a fiber per connection.

#### listen_tls

```khora
pub fn listen_tls<'er>(router: Router<'er>, port: Int, certificate: String, key: String) ->() with { scope: Scope } raises 'er + HttpError + TlsError + ChildFailed
```

The same, over TLS.

Takes the certificate chain and the key as PEM rather than as paths: a
server that reads its own files has decided where they live, and the two
deployments that matter — a file on disk and a secret handed in by the
platform — disagree about that.

The configuration is released when the caller's scope ends, which for a
server is usually the program's.

#### bound

```khora
pub fn bound<'ef>(port: Int) -> Int raises HttpError
```

A listening socket on `port`, announced by the caller.

#### serve_secured

```khora
pub fn serve_secured<'er>(router: Router<'er>, server: Int, settings: TlsServer) ->() with { nursery: Nursery } raises 'er + HttpError
```

`serve_forever` over TLS: accepts, handshakes, and serves on a fiber
each.

A failed handshake ends that fiber quietly rather than the loop — on a
public port it is the ordinary case, not an incident.

#### serve_forever

```khora
pub fn serve_forever<'er>(router: Router<'er>, server: Int) ->() with { nursery: Nursery } raises 'er + HttpError
```

Accepts connections on `server` until the process stops.

`listen` is the one to call: it binds the port and then this. Taking an
already-bound socket is for a caller that wants to bind it themselves —
a test on port zero, a socket inherited from a supervisor.

#### answer_on

```khora
pub fn answer_on<'er>(router: Router<'er>, transport: Transport) ->() raises 'er
```

Answers every request on one connection, until the client stops.

**Written against the public [`Connection`], with nothing reserved.** A
framework of a different shape writes this loop itself and is not missing
anything: the reading, the framing and the refusals are all above.

## Functions

### percent_decode

```khora
pub fn percent_decode(text: String) -> String
```

`%20` becomes a space, and so does `+`.

A `%` not followed by two hex digits stays a literal `%`. Refusing the
whole parameter would be defensible and is not what any browser or server
does, and a query string is not the place to be the only strict one.

The decoded form is never longer than the encoded one, so a buffer of the
input's length is always enough and there is nothing to grow.

### parse

```khora
pub fn parse(text: String) -> Option<Request>
```

A request read off the wire.

### default_limit

```khora
pub fn default_limit() -> Int
```

The most a request may be, headers and body together, unless a caller
says otherwise.

Eight kilobytes is what a buffer costs per connection, and a connection is
what a fiber costs — so this is the number that decides how many callers a
server can hold, not a guess about how big a request is. `Connection::holding`
takes another.

The buffer is allocated once at this size and never grows, which is what
makes a lying `Content-Length` harmless: the header is a promise about what
is coming, not an instruction to allocate.

**Eight kilobytes is a policy, not a limit of the parser.** Nothing here
recurses per byte or per line, so a larger request is refused because the
limit says so rather than because the parser cannot manage it: a
39,808-byte request carrying 2,001 headers parses and answers when the
limit is raised to admit it.

The number stays at eight kilobytes anyway, which is what nginx and most
others allow, because the question it answers changed rather than
disappeared. It is no longer "how much can we survive" but "how much may an
unauthenticated client make a server hold", and that is a smaller number
than the one the stack would now permit.

### over_socket

```khora
pub fn over_socket(connection: Int) -> Transport
```

A transport over a plain socket.

### over_tls

```khora
pub fn over_tls(connection: TlsConnection) -> Transport
```

A transport over a secured connection.

The socket is the TLS connection's now — `secure` took it and `shut` closes
it — so there is nothing here that closes it a second time.

### request_length

```khora
pub fn request_length(bytes: Array<U8>, filled: Int) -> Int
```

How long the whole request should be, or negative while the headers are
still arriving.

**The framing primitive.** A reader needs to know when to stop, and HTTP
answers that in two parts: the headers end at a blank line, and
`Content-Length` says how much follows. Getting it wrong is not a bug that
shows up in testing — it is a request truncated at a packet boundary, or two
requests read as one — which is why this is exported rather than left for
each framework to derive again.

[`Connection`] is this with a buffer around it, and is what most callers
want.

### matches

```khora
pub fn matches(pattern: String, path: String) -> Option<Params>
```

Whether `path` matches `pattern`, and what its `:name` segments bound.

`/analyze/:id` against `/analyze/acc_9921` binds `id`. `None` when the
shapes disagree, which is how the router moves on to the next route.

Exported so a program can route somewhere other than through `Router` —
a WebSocket upgrade, a second listener — without reimplementing the one
piece of matching that has to agree with the server's.

### default_answer_limit

```khora
pub fn default_answer_limit() -> Int
```

How much of an answer this client will hold, when nobody says otherwise.

64 KiB, and it is a buffer allocated per call rather than per connection —
a hundred fibers each making a request is a hundred of these at once, which
is why it is not measured in megabytes. `HttpClient::bounded` raises it for
a caller who knows they are fetching something bigger.

### default_answer_timeout

```khora
pub fn default_answer_timeout() -> Int
```

How long to wait for bytes that are not arriving, in milliseconds.

**On both paths now.** It was the plain one only, because
`set_receive_timeout` takes a socket and a TLS session owns its socket
rather than handing it back -- so a TLS server that accepted the connection
and then said nothing held the fiber until the process ended.
`std::net::tls` sets the deadline on the socket underneath, and `dial` uses
it for `https` exactly as it does for `http`.

### parse_url

```khora
pub fn parse_url(text: String) -> Option<Url>
```

Reads `https://host:port/path?query`.

**Only what a client needs to dial and ask.** No fragment, because a
fragment never leaves the browser; no userinfo, because credentials in a
URL are deprecated and accepting them would mean deciding how to encode
them; and no normalisation of the path, because a server may have signed
exactly the bytes it was given.
